stem:
At a ten-week booking visit, a GP reviews a woman with laboratory-confirmed beta-thalassaemia trait; her ferritin is normal. Her partner, the baby’s father, is well. His full blood count from a recent insurance medical showed haemoglobin 152 g/L and MCV 88 fL. The couple want to understand the risk to the baby before deciding about invasive fetal testing.

Which investigation should the GP arrange next?

options.label: A
options.text: No partner testing, because his normal MCV excludes a relevant trait
options.explanation: Some clinically important carrier states, notably HbS, have normal red-cell indices; combined with her beta-thalassaemia trait, HbS would put the fetus at risk of sickle–beta-thalassaemia.

options.label: B
options.text: Partner ferritin first, then haemoglobin studies only if it is low
options.explanation: Ferritin addresses iron deficiency, not carrier status; waiting on it delays the result that determines fetal risk.

options.label: C
options.text: Chorionic villus sampling now, on the basis of the maternal trait
options.explanation: Invasive testing is offered after both parents are shown to carry relevant traits; the partner’s status is not yet known.

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal beta-globin gene sequencing before the partner is tested
options.explanation: Her trait is already established; defining her mutation helps later fetal diagnosis but does not tell the couple whether the fetus is at risk.

options.label: E
options.text: Arrange his haemoglobin studies now, despite a normal MCV
options.explanation: When one partner is a carrier, the other needs haemoglobin studies (HPLC or electrophoresis) promptly, because a normal MCV does not exclude traits such as HbS.

context: When a pregnant woman carries beta-thalassaemia trait, test her partner with haemoglobin studies promptly; normal red-cell indices do not exclude traits such as HbS.
